full_judgment:
10. The said writ petitions were heard analogously and those Rules were discharged on 12-6-2012 with observations that the writ petitioners are at liberty to invoke the proper forum as provided under Section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. As per the said observations, the petitioners (except in writ petition Nos.2581/2014 and 2580/2014) filed Land Survey Suit Nos. 8 of 2013, 15/2013, 14/2013, 10/2013, 11/2013, 13/2013, 16/2013, 18/2013 and before the Land Survey Tribunal Dhaka Mohanagor which is still pending. 

 20. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing with learned Advocate Mr Md Imam Hasan (in writ petition No. 2581 of 2014) on behalf of the respondent Nos.11-12 submits that neither the petitioner made any statements against the RAJUK in the writ petition nor sought any relief against the RAJUK and RAJUK is no way connected with the subject matter of the instant writ petition and a such Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 22. The moot question to be considered in these Rules is whether acquisition of the land of petitioners has been made for public purpose or not and whether such acquisition has been made following the due procedure. 

 24. We note that since the petitioners have changed the nature of the land in question to be their own land, we are of the view whether the land of the petitioners falls within the acquisition is a disputed question of fact and such question cannot be resolved without measurement and taking evidence within is beyond the purview of the writ jurisdiction. Reliance is placed on the decision in Nasirullah and another vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 61 DLR 119. 

 26. It is now well established that Courts can examine the purpose of the acquisition to determine whether or not it has been made for a public purpose. The Privy Council in Hamabi Framjee Petit vs Secretary of State for India in Council, 42 Ind App 44 : (AIR 1914 PC 20), stated the law in these words. 

 27. Again; the Supreme court in State of Bombay vs RS Nanji, (S) AIR, 1956 SC 294, laid down : 

 28. From these, it follows that it is open to this Court sitting under writ jurisdiction provided under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh to determine whether or not the acquisition in the present cases have been made for a public purpose. The point to be determined in each case relating to the private and public interest has been held in the case of State of Bihar vs Sir Kameshwar Singh, reported in AIR 1952 SC 252 where it was observed that : 

 "As between individuals, no necessity, however great, no exigency, however imminent, no improvement, however valuable, no refusal, however un-neighborly, no obstinacy, however unreasonable, no offers of compensation, however extravagant, can compel or require any man to part with an inch of his estate." 

 31. Nichols in his well known book "The Law of Eminent Domain" stated that: 

 32. When the property is acquired for project to be implemented by the Government, the object/purpose of acquisition is treated as for public. Whereas, when the property is acquired for project to be implemented and funded by body other than Government and the project is for public good or public use, the object/purpose of acquisition is treated as public interest. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Gias Uddin Chowdhury, 2012 BLD (AD) 1 = 17 BLC (AD) 14, their Lordships observed: 

 "As soon as a piece of land is acquired in accordance with law the owner is deprived of his right. A citizen holds his property, subject always to the right of the sovereign to take it for a public purpose. This right is called eminent domain. The right of eminent domain is the right of the sovereign State through its regular agencies." 

 33. In the light of the finding made herein-above, this Court of the view that this Court will not interfere with the acquisition since the acquisition was for public purpose and there is nothing which shows that law was violated in the process of acquisition.
